answer.line: The end methyl's enolate reaches the other C=O and closes a six-membered ring; warming then loses water to the conjugated enone.

steps: List the carbons that can become enolates: the two end methyls, C1 and C7, and the CH2 groups beside the carbonyls, C3 and C5.
Count each ring. The C1 enolate attacking the C6 carbonyl closes six atoms. The C3 enolate attacking C6 closes only four, far too strained.
Warming dehydrates the beta-hydroxy ketone and puts the C=C in line with the C=O: 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.

choices.note: This five-membered enone comes from hexane-2,5-dione. Heptane-2,6-dione is one carbon longer, so its ring closes six.
Six-membered ring, C=C conjugated with the C=O.
The ring size is right. But the methyl from the second ketone is gone, and so is the C=C that dehydration makes.
Right ring, right atoms. But the C=C sits out of line with the C=O. Dehydration gives the conjugated enone, which is more stable.
Keeping both C=O groups is what an acylation does, and even then they end up 1,3, not side by side. In an aldol, one C=O is the target and becomes the new C=C.

lockIt: Intramolecular aldol: close the five or six ring, then lose water to the conjugated enone.

playWith.label: Tree, the alpha carbon: pick the aldol condensation and play the move, enolate attack and then water lost

visual.alt: Heptane-2,6-dione with three carbons marked: C1, whose enolate attacks; C6, the carbonyl it attacks; and C3, which would close only a four-membered ring. With NaOH and warming it gives 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one, its C=C in line with the C=O.
visual.caption: Count from C1 to C6: six atoms. From C3 you get four, too strained to close.
